description: GenAIus is a team of three software engineering students combining AI, data analysis, backend development, and web design. For Flame in Freefall, we aim to make NASA’s combustion research easier to explore and compare through source-grounded insights, clear visualizations, and transparent limitations.
summary:
GenAIus helps researchers explore how fire behaves in microgravity using traceable NASA evidence. Developed for Flame in Freefall, it connects a 24-study catalog with interactive analysis of 403 BASS-II and FLEX test runs, while keeping different experiments and evidence types separate.

Users can compare material measurements, check whether selected conditions are supported by indexed tests, explore experimental FLEX model estimates, and investigate published SAFFIRE observations. An evidence assistant combines deterministic table calculations, BM25 report retrieval, and optional source-grounded LLM explanations.

Our contribution is a unified workflow that distinguishes measured results, derived values, model estimates, and missing evidence. Every result leads back to its source, helping users identify relevant experiments and research gaps without presenting predictions as safety certifications.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

GeNAIus is an interactive research dashboard for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It helps combustion researchers and spacecraft or habitat engineering teams find relevant NASA experiments, compare recorded conditions, and identify where available evidence ends.

The project brings together experimental tables, scientific reports, and published case-study findings while preserving their different origins and limitations.

HOW IT WORKS

Material Lab explores 129 BASS-II solid-material test runs. Users select materials and geometries, compare valid gas measurements, and inspect distributions and oxygen coverage. Initial and final measurements remain distinct, and missing or invalid values are never silently converted to zero.

Fire Animation provides a conceptual illustration rather than a physical simulation. Its scenario checker labels evidence coverage as TESTED, PARTIAL, or GAP within indexed sources. A separate FLEX panel provides experimental Ridge regression estimates of the burning-rate constant and Logistic Regression extinction scores. Predictions outside supported conditions are blocked; extinction scores are not calibrated fire-safety probabilities.

The SAFFIRE Case Study connects published test conditions, gas results, and smoke observations. For VI-3, it distinguishes reported timestamps from our derived 344-second interval between ignition and the authors’ selected smoke-concentration criterion. It does not interpret this interval as an operational spacecraft alarm delay.

Data provides a 24-study catalog and access to 403 core test runs: 129 BASS-II and 274 FLEX records. CFI, SAFFIRE-II, and report-derived case evidence remain separate. Users can inspect records, compare tests, export subsets, and trace source files through provenance information.

The Evidence Assistant calculates supported table summaries deterministically. BM25 retrieves relevant report passages, while an optional OpenRouter-hosted NVIDIA Nemotron model produces source-grounded explanations. Schema, citation, and numerical checks can reject invalid responses and return deterministic evidence instead.

TECHNOLOGIES

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, and Canvas. FLEX training uses scikit-learn pipelines with feature transformations, StandardScaler, Ridge, and LogisticRegression, evaluated with grouped condition splits. Report retrieval uses BM25 lexical search.

ORIGINAL CONTRIBUTION AND IMPACT

Our contribution is connecting measurements, document evidence, scenario coverage, and separate model estimates in one traceable workflow. Users can distinguish what NASA measured, what our software calculated, what a model estimated, and what remains unsupported.

We prioritized experimental context, units, missing-data handling, reproducibility, and transparent AI use. GeNAIus supports research and further investigation; it does not certify materials, predict crew exposure, or establish spacecraft fire safety.
